newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Founder joins chorus of critical Brierley s/holders.
newsitem.headline: Founder joins chorus of critical Brierley s/holders.

text.p: Brierley Investments Ltd chairman Bob Matthew said on Thursday 1995/96 was unspectacular but "highly satisfactory" for BIL -- but shareholders, including founder Sir Ron Brierley, thought otherwise.

A succession of shareholders at the annual meeting, attended by over 1,000, criticised returns from the New Zealand investment company which provided spectacular results up until the 1987 share crash when its share price was over NZ$5 (US$3.57) against $1.32 today.
Investment adviser Oliver Saint, proxy holder for an Auckland investor, said a printout of BIL's price was a tremendous 'L' shape "and the horizontal line seems to go on for ever and ever".
"Nine years and we have got no progress, and that I think is one reason why she is concerned," Saint said.
Another shareholder said the company had been "hijacked by its executive staff and directors", and called for an independent review of its performance.
Matthew denied the company had been hijacked but said consideration would be given to a review. BIL reported net profit of NZ$310 million in the year to June, down from $432 million a year earlier.
President Sir Ron Brierley told Reuters after the meeting the shareholder who referred to the "long horizontal line" in the share price explained the rancour of the meeting.
"No one is more acutely aware of that (the flat share price) than myself," Brierley told Reuters.
Brierley, regarded as a hero by investors, is today more active in GPG Ltd than BIL, but still has four million shares and is listed among the top three shareholders in the company.
"One is not being critical or making any particularly profound comment, but it is a plain fact of life that the shares just haven't gone up -- in fact they have gone down."

Other shareholders complained about non-performing assets such as recently-listed British hotel group Thistle, where BIL has sold its stake down to 46 percent from 70 percent, and loss-making U.S. assets.
BIL's shares have risen from $1.24 last year but have struggled below $2 all through the 1990s. But Matthew said disgruntled shareholders were being nostalgic.

"In terms of return, the accent needs to be on the extent to which we are enhancing the value of the underlying business," he said adding that value during the year to June 30 had been enhanced by over $700 million.
A year ago BIL said it aimed to enhance shareholder value -- profits, dividends and unrealised gains -- by $2 billion by June 1998 but Matthew noted the figure was a target, not a promise.

Asked to comment on Matthew's claim that the year had been highly satisfactory, Brierley said: "Well, they are good words but from the shareholders' point of view it's not reflected in the share price and hasn't been reflected for a long time, and quite honestly that is a legitimate cause of compaint.
"Whether or not it is something that BIL has total control of, or has any control of, is another matter, but the plain fact is that the shares hadn't performed for a long period of time."
